input.question: If the coriolis effect makes hurricanes/typhoons swirl in different directions, what exactly happens when storms cross the equator? Do they begin to slow and weaken?
input.ground_truth: Look at [this chart](_URL_0_). Hurricanes don't cross the equator! They don't even form very close to the equator, because the Coriolis effect doesn't exist at the equator and is very small at small latitudes. As a storm approaches the equator, it either loses intensity or turns away because there is no driving force there to keep it going.

Question: If the coriolis effect makes hurricanes/typhoons swirl in different directions, what exactly happens when storms cross the equator? Do they begin to slow and weaken?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a bathtub and you swirl the water around with your finger. The water goes in a circle, right? Now, pretend the bathtub has a big line down the middle (that’s the equator). If you make a whirlpool on one side of the line, it spins one way. If you make one on the other side, it spins the other way because of something called the "Coriolis effect."

Now, if your whirlpool (which is like a hurricane or typhoon) starts moving and crosses that big line (the equator), it has to change the way it spins! It’s like if you were spinning around and suddenly had to switch which way you spin. So, as the storm crosses the equator, it might get a little confused and start to slow down or change direction a bit. But it doesn’t always get weaker—sometimes it just changes the way it spins.

So, when a storm crosses the equator, it can change the way it swirls because of the Coriolis effect, but it doesn’t always get weaker. It just gets a little mixed up!
